This document introduces the official catalog of the highest-energy cosmic rays observed by the Pierre Auger Observatory throughout its operational Phase I. The catalog, which includes 1000 events with energies exceeding $10^{17.8}$ eV, was developed to support the publication of the Observatory's sensitivity study. Event details are provided with an energy measurement uncertainty of less than 15%.

Current research in deep object detection has increasingly focused on uncertainty quantification, yet most existing techniques fail to address detectors trained on limited datasets. This study introduces a straightforward yet effective approach to estimate uncertainty for deep detectors. The method involves training a single detector and utilizing it to generate predictions for both test images and training images (treated as unlabeled). While the training-based predictions are inherently biased, they serve as the foundation for constructing an analytical estimator of the posterior distribution. This proposed estimator is designed to be computationally efficient, requiring only a negligible fraction of a standard inference pass. Furthermore, it demonstrates superior accuracy compared to traditional estimators, which are often based on the assumption of a Gaussian posterior distribution.

Forecasting a traffic network's future state is essential for applications such as traffic control and navigation. While most existing research relies on traffic count data, this data is often sparse and delayed, whereas video surveillance can offer more frequent updates. This paper introduces a novel approach to network traffic prediction that segments a traffic network into individual moving parts and predicts future states for each segment independently. By utilizing a convolutional neural network (CNN) to extract features from video frames, the method employs a dynamic network structure to account for varying numbers of segments and their attributes. The approach is evaluated using both simulated and real-world datasets, demonstrating that it achieves superior performance in predicting networks compared to state-of-the-art baselines.

We introduce a rewriting mechanism for terms belonging to Gray classes—subsets of groups characterized by an additional involution $\bar{\phantom{x}}$ satisfying $\overline{e}^{-1} = \overline{e}^{-1}$ and a specified anti-automorphism $e \mapsto e^t$ satisfying $\overline{e}^t = \overline{e}^t$. Rewriting systems are constructed to be compatible with these Gray class axioms, and it is demonstrated that this compatibility is both necessary and sufficient to guarantee termination. Furthermore, applying this result yields a quadratic-time algorithm to determine consistency within various types of rings and to compute the half of a Gröbner-Shirase basis for ideals situated within a semigroup ring.

Accurately segmenting the hippocampus is crucial for diagnosing and monitoring various neurological conditions, particularly epilepsy. This study introduces a fully automated method for analyzing hippocampal segmentation in patients with temporal lobe epilepsy (TLE) and Alzheimer's disease (AD) using deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs). The methodology employs four distinct CNN architectures—FCN-1024, FCN-512, FCN-32, and FCN-16—to generate segmentation maps. The segmentation process involves applying these four architectures to detect the hippocampus, followed by a classification step that distinguishes between AD and TLE based on segmented metrics. The findings indicate that the fully automated approach yields a Dice coefficient of 0.836 for the segmentation task and a classification accuracy of 0.82 for distinguishing AD from TLE.

We introduce a novel quantum algorithm designed to address the classical mode problem, utilizing the principle of amplitude amplification. This method offers an advantage over classical algorithms, achieving a time complexity of $O(\sqrt{N})$ compared to the classical $O(N)$ requirement. The system's functionality is verified through execution on both the IBM quantum cloud and a local quantum simulator. Additionally, our approach leverages non-classical features to resolve specific instances of the classic pigeonhole problem.

This paper introduces a Monte Carlo code designed to simulate the trajectories of cosmic ray particles with energies ranging from 100 MeV to 100 GeV as they traverse the Earth's atmosphere and magnetosphere, specifically for low Earth orbit (LEO) altitudes between 300 and 2,000 km. The study evaluates the contributions of both primary cosmic rays and secondary particles generated through atmospheric interactions. The simulation incorporates the International Reference Magnetospheric model (IGRF) alongside the NOAA solar flux indices. The results indicate that the intensity of these particles exhibits strong dependencies on both geographic location and the phase of the solar cycle.

Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have become a vital tool for analyzing graph-structured data, yet existing models often rely on simplistic assumptions and struggle to adapt to complex real-world scenarios. This paper introduces a comprehensive design framework for GNNs that begins with a global pyramid-style shrinking process and proceeds to a local reconfiguration of graph topology connections. Our global shrinking model employs weighted aggregation to generate node embeddings, effectively mitigating the impact of graph sparsity. Subsequently, a novel strategy for reconfiguring topological links is employed to refine embedding quality by dynamically adjusting the adjacency matrix. This adaptive approach establishes a powerful pipeline for extracting high-quality graph representations. We validate our proposed framework across diverse datasets and complex tasks, demonstrating its superior performance compared to current state-of-the-art methods.

We suggest a new method for managing privacy while analyzing large matrices, drawing on the well-established Huber technique for robust statistics. This approach is applicable to two primary tasks: completing low-rank matrices and extracting matrix factorization. Our strategy is robust against the presence of non-private data and incorporates well-designed, private algorithms specifically for these two tasks. By utilizing Hubs-based procedures, the system effectively mitigates the negative impacts of outliers, whereas traditional, non-robust methods fail in such scenarios. Furthermore, we demonstrate that our approach scales efficiently to handle large datasets. We also provide a rigorous theoretical analysis, including bounds on the number of queries required and the privacy guarantees offered by the Huber framework.

Interstellar dust is responsible for extinction, emission, and polarization across all wavelengths of light. While the interstellar medium (ISM) is often sparse, it is crucial for understanding the interstellar extinction curve, emission spectra from objects like the Orion Nebula, and polarized light from sources such as the Orion-B161 nebula. In the dense regions of the ISM, dust behaves similarly to that in the laboratory; however, in the sparse areas, dust grains are significantly modified by environmental factors. To address this, we introduce the Astrodust+PAH model, which utilizes a cohesive framework to represent dust grains and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs) within the sparse interstellar medium. This model relies on a modified Mie theory calculation using spheroidal grains, which are charged to align with magnetic fields. Their size distribution follows a log-normal curve, and their optical properties are derived from the Draine & Lee (1997) theory. To account for shape alterations in the near-infrared caused by grain charging, we employ a dielectric function based on the Draine & Lee (1997) model. Additionally, we utilize the Fomenkov et al. (2019) model to represent PAH emission. This unified model successfully reproduces the emission spectra of the Orion nebula and the dust polarization observed in the Orion-B161 nebula.

This study presents the discovery of a massive planet located within the disk surrounding CIDA 1, an extremely low-mass star with a mass of 0.075 M$_{\odot}$. The planet was identified through high-resolution ALMA observations, revealing a peak brightness temperature of 1000 K and a mass of 1.5 M$_{\oplus}$ at a separation of 0.12 AU. This system represents the first confirmed case of a planet around a star with such minimal mass, offering a unique opportunity to investigate the formation and evolution of planets in regimes where stellar and sub-stellar objects converge. Furthermore, the system's properties align with a scenario involving planet formation via core accretion, suggesting that this process can persist even in environments with extremely depleted dust content.

This paper introduces a novel image partitioning framework that integrates image restoration techniques. The method employs an original energy function, which is optimized through a straightforward variational approach. The function is minimized using a new iterative algorithm that combines K-means clustering with an iterative shrinkage operator. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated on two key tasks: partitioning noisy images and simultaneously denoising and segmenting them. The results indicate that the method produces high-quality outcomes and is particularly advantageous when applied to images with significant noise levels.

Abstract Interpretation, a technique for formally analyzing software systems, relies on the soundness property that ensures all system behaviors are captured. This soundness is achieved by replacing a program's concrete semantics with a more abstract representation. Abstract domains, which define the shapes of these generalized semantics, are constructed using specific operators. Historically, abstract domain designers have been compelled to independently address both ascending and descending operators, a requirement that often complicates the design process unnecessarily. This paper introduces a novel methodology that separates the construction of abstract domains from operators governing the rising and falling phases. By decoupling these rising and falling operators, the development of new abstract domains becomes a significantly simpler and more intuitive task.

Phonons serve as vital mediators of structural and electronic phenomena in condensed matter, yet their entanglement with other degrees of freedom renders phenomena like phononic topological order elusive. This study investigates the topological ordering of phonons in the perovskite ceramic BaTiO$_3$ under photoexcitation. We demonstrate that intense light drives the emergence of a distinct topological phase characterized by a non-zero Chern number, a state not observed in the ground state. This light-induced topological phase transition stems from the dynamic contraction of the phononic bandgap and a concurrent rise in the anharmonicity of lattice vibrations. Furthermore, we establish that such topological phases can be accessed in BaTiO$_3$ and BaSrTiO$_3$ through thermal fluctuations even at elevated temperatures. These findings underscore the potential of tunable topological phononics in advanced perovskite materials.

Outlier detection is a fundamental task in data mining, yet it remains difficult in general metric spaces because traditional methods relying on density struggle without a defined data distribution. This paper introduces a new outlier identification approach based on weighted proximity graphs. The proposed method evaluates local density by analyzing the distribution of edge lengths on a graph constructed from the dataset. By utilizing a weighted graph, we can accurately pinpoint outliers in regions where data points are tightly clustered alongside normal points in the broader space. Experimental results across various datasets confirm that this approach is both efficient and accurate, outperforming existing methods in the specific context where similar points coexist with widely dispersed outliers.

Additionally, the mirror can emit its own radiation due to the atom's motion. This study examines two theoretical frameworks—natural supersymmetry (NUS) and split (divided) supersymmetry (DUS)—utilizing the 13 TeV proton-proton collision dataset from the Large Hadron Collider, which corresponds to an integrated luminosity of 139 fb$^{-1}$. The analysis focuses on events characterized by at least two jets with high transverse momentum and significant missing transverse momentum. We evaluate the compatibility of experimental observations with specific decay modes for neutral superpartners, focusing on scenarios where neutralinos decompose into a photon pair, a pair of $Z$ bosons, or a pair of Higgs bosons. Our results indicate that the decay channels associated with $Z$ bosons and Higgs bosons are strongly excluded by the data, whereas supersymmetry models within the natural framework remain viable. Conversely, split supersymmetry models are excluded by these results.

This work presents a "diagnostic" approach to identifying financial bubbles, diverging from traditional methods by "logically" analyzing expectations regarding an asset's fundamental value. We introduce a new, generalizable probabilistic model for determining the termination time of a bubble, characterizing it as mean-reverting and random. This analytical framework is both mathematically rigorous and adaptable to specific empirical scenarios. Within this approach, we define two distinct metrics for bubble detection: the risk of bursting and the mean duration until termination. We demonstrate that these diagnostics can be effectively applied to analyze historical bubble events and potential future scenarios.

Product evaluation is a fundamental aspect of online commerce, where user-generated content significantly influences purchasing decisions. While existing research predominantly targets product classification using product titles or descriptions, this work proposes a novel approach for recommending products based on reviews. We introduce the Sentiment-sensitive Interactive Fusion Network (SIFN), a neural network designed to extract salient features from reviews by accounting for sentiment-specific nuances. We validate our method on the Amazon dataset, where it outperforms state-of-the-art methods in identifying relevant products. Additionally, a detailed case study demonstrates the effectiveness of our sentiment-aware fusion mechanism.

Code-switching (CS) is a prevalent linguistic feature in mixed-language environments, yet it remains a significant hurdle in machine translation research. This study investigates the utility of lexical substitutions for augmenting data within English-Arabic translation models. We introduce a novel, lexicon-based algorithm that generates contextual word replacements and assess its effectiveness in augmenting Arabic-CW switched datasets. Our evaluation compares this approach against a widely used back-translation augmentation technique. Results indicate that our proposed method yields superior performance, as ascertained through improvements in both automated metrics and human assessment scores.

The article demonstrates that any subgroup within the group of diffeomorphisms of a closed surface which leaves a single point fixed belongs to the class of non-Roelcke precompact groups. This finding extends earlier work by Megrelishvili and Raikov, corresponding to the case of homeomorphisms.

Connectivity of connectable cosets plays a crucial role in the coset conjecture regarding connectable deformations. We demonstrate that generalized $\\lambda$-deformations are indeed connectable by establishing that their connected components are connectable cosets. Consequently, we propose a set of guidelines for constructing connected generalized $\\lambda$-deformations.

This approach addresses the challenge of automatically converting a shape-based mesh into a hexagonal lattice. The method's primary objective is to generate a valid hexagonal structure that closely approximates the original surface while maintaining a high degree of topological simplicity. The algorithm operates in a two-stage process: initially, it analyzes the surface geometry to determine an appropriate level of detail, and subsequently, it constructs the corresponding hexagonal lattice. The system demonstrates exceptional performance, capable of processing a mesh of up to 58 tetrahedra per second on a single core of a standard desktop processor.

Relation Extraction (RE) entails identifying relationships between entity pairs within textual data. This research addresses the challenge of detecting incomplete relationships between entities in text, a problem modeled as determining the optimal link between two entities in a Knowledge Graph (KG). To address this, we introduce an end-to-end framework that leverages state-of-the-art Link Prediction (LP) models to bolster RE performance. This approach utilizes a shared LP model, trained concurrently with the RE system on a set of candidate KG links. By leveraging the LP model to refine the representation of entity pairs through its inference on this shared link prediction task, the system effectively leverages LP performance to upgrade the RE system. Consequently, this mechanism refines the final classification of relationships. Empirical evaluations across three standard RE benchmarks confirm that the approach yields significant performance improvements.

This work introduces a generalized analytical formula for the delay of power converters, accommodating arbitrary efficiency and input-output voltage ratios. The proposed model is validated through experimental data gathered from a 1-W DC-DC buck converter, with final parameter values ascertained via the Matlab Curve Fitting Toolkit.

Continuity is a fundamental concept in analysis that is often employed to streamline the derivation of results. However, in many mathematical derivations, continuity is utilized in ways that are overly restrictive, preventing its application to broader scenarios. We propose a new concept, "coarse-grained continuity," designed to accommodate scenarios where classical continuity is too limiting. This approach is applicable to the exploration-exploitation dilemma in reinforcement learning (RL). We demonstrate that coarse-grained continuity is sufficient to guarantee that an RL environment's finite approximation yields a finite approximation for any algorithm. This finding supports the creation of theoretically grounded algorithms for real-world RL challenges. Furthermore, we outline the key characteristics of coarse-grained continuity and establish its relationship with total variation distance under specific constraints. We also establish that coarse-grained continuity is preserved when a sub-Markov kernel is projected through continuous mappings. These findings are presented within an abstract framework, with specific examples provided using standard analysis topologies.

Animations are a fundamental visual category in contemporary life, ranging from moving traffic and flowing rivers to and people walking crowds. Yet, defining what constitutes an animation remains unclear. To investigate this, we conducted an fMRI study involving 17 participants, examining brain activity in the ventral temporal cortex in response to real-life animations, static images, and natural scenes. Our results revealed that the neural signature distinguishing animations from static images is the reverse of the signature separating static images from natural scenes. This finding supports the hypothesis that an animation's neural impact is a combination of its scene content and its lack of stasis. Consequently, determining whether something is an animation depends less on what it depicts and more on how it fails to remain static.

This study introduces a new class of arrangement-preserving filters designed for multidimensional data processing in signal restoration and inverse problems. These filters effectively eliminate noise from data represented as signals on the finite elements of a mesh while maintaining crucial geometric properties, such as monotonicity and convexity. The filter's construction relies on a novel, computationally efficient formula for calculating weights using a generic convex optimization framework. The proposed filtering methods are evaluated through a series of tests involving signals associated with 2D and 3D finite element meshes.

This study investigates the corona within the black hole binary MAXI J1535-571 during its 2018 outburst, utilizing data from the Insight-HXMT mission. By analyzing the outburst's type-C quasi-periodic oscillations (QPOs) and their corresponding X-ray spectral properties, we aimed to trace the evolutionary path of the corona. Our findings reveal a hard-state corona that is both hot and compact, characterized by temperatures ranging from 100 to 150 keV and a size of approximately 100 gravitational radii. As the state transitions to soft, the corona becomes cooler, larger, and more extended. Specifically, during the hard-to-soft transition (HS-SSS) QPO phase, the corona expands to roughly 200 gravitational radii with a temperature of about 10 keV; conversely, in the soft-state (soft-state QPO phase), it is even more expansive, extending beyond 300 gravitational radii. These results align with the standard paradigm of a soft, thick accretion disk enveloping a cold, diffuse outer corona. Furthermore, the observed QPO frequency in the soft-state matches the theoretical prediction for the maximum orbital period at the outer edge of the accretion disk.

The paper introduces a fresh methodology for socially motivated empowerment transfer designed to generate dependable re-responsive behaviors in multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL). A foundational element of this approach is the Dependable Re-Responsive Social Intrinsic Motivation (DREAM) function, which is engineered to consistently recognize an agent's partner actions and establish a motivation profile that fosters complex, collaborative multi-agent behaviors. The motivation is derived through the empowerment framework, which quantifies the potential influence an agent can exert on its environment. The DREAM function specifically assesses three dimensions: the partner's available empowerment, the agent's own current empowerment, and the degree of alignment between their respective motivations. The primary objective of this function is to drive the agent to mimic its partner's potential and the congruence of their motivations. The study demonstrates that an agent utilizing DREAM for intrinsic motivation can reliably acquire transferable empowerment and maintain consistent, stable cooperation patterns. Furthermore, the work illustrates that this learned motivation enables highly dependable social adaptation to dynamic partner behaviors, ensuring the agent can effectively respond to shifting motivations and operational goals.

We introduce a contrastive learning strategy designed to create robust substance representations by distinguishing between real observations and synthetic simulations. This method employs physics-driven simulations to generate contextual features that enhance material identification capabilities. By leveraging these synthetic data to train a discriminator capable of distinguishing authenticity, we harness the network's ability to reject falsities during inference, thereby anchoring substance embeddings in realistic representational spaces. This approach enables few-shot identification of unknown materials within arbitrary scenes. Validated on synthetic environments and real-world data, our results demonstrate that the model successfully identifies substances with zero training examples of the target item and zero training shots for the category, relying solely on extensive training data for general substance categories.

Lie 2-algebras, defined as crossed modules of groups, serve as three-dimensional L-infinity algebras and function as powerful tools for modeling homotopy-theoretic phenomena. This article provides an accessible introduction to Lie 2-algebras, covering their various equivalent representations and standard constructions. Additionally, an appendix is included that offers some non-trivial examples.

This work introduces a novel, end-to-end architecture for local feature detection and descriptor generation, leveraging the strength of self-attention mechanisms. Unlike prior methods, our single unified model simultaneously handles descriptor generation and matching without requiring a separate matching stage. This design is particularly effective at descriptor creation for low-quality images, including those with low resolution, and facilitates matching even in challenging scenarios involving low resolution and low contrast. Empirical results demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses existing state-of-the-art techniques across various difficult test cases.

Accurately measuring the Sun's vector magnetic field is essential for understanding solar dynamics and predicting space weather. However, the complex nature of the task has led to systematic errors in the derived measurements. This study examines bias in the magnetic field data obtained from various instruments, specifically focusing on the relationship between the longitudinal and transverse components. We analyze a comprehensive dataset comprising magnetic field measurements from all six satellites in the Solar Heliospheric Magnetic Field Experiment (SHMFE) fleet, including those equipped with vector magnetometers. Our analysis reveals a bias in the magnetic field data, which is most pronounced in instruments with lower resolution. We attribute this systematic error to limitations in resolution and the presence of noise. To mitigate this issue, we introduce a new method for reducing bias in the magnetic field data, which significantly improves the overall quality of the measurements. We validate the effectiveness of this method by applying it to a subset of the magnetic field data, specifically to the region of the solar active region AR12737, which is known for its complex magnetic field structure.

This paper proposes an innovative demand side control approach for independent energy users, utilizing a collective game to establish a daily energy usage schedule. In this framework, users compete by submitting usage plans, with a social welfare function designed to incentivize reducing peak loads. To refine this schedule, a real-time charging mechanism is introduced alongside an adaptive bidding process that adjusts bids based on the deviations between planned and actual consumption. Theoretical analysis confirms the existence and Nash stability of an equilibrium within the proposed game. Furthermore, the efficacy of this method is demonstrated through a case study comparing it against traditional demand side control strategies.

Using Rastall gravity to explore the complete thermal emission of a charged black string, we analyze the first- and second-law relationships governing its first law of black hole thermodynamics. By examining the first law, we derive the mass formula for the string and subsequently apply the second law to determine its entropy. The analysis reveals that the first law holds only when the Rastall parameter is non-positive, whereas the second law imposes no such restriction. We further investigate the thermodynamic stability of the system, finding that configurations with a non-negative Rastall parameter are stable, while those with negative values are unstable. Additionally, the study shows the first law is valid exclusively for adiabatic processes.

This work investigates how spectral measures and spectral distributions behave in von Neumann's Ergodic Theorem, specifically examining the impact of spectral gaps and regions of spectral concentration on the convergence rate of weakly mixing systems. Additionally, the study explores the relationship between von Neumann's and Birkhoff's Ergodic Theorems from the perspective of spectral analysis.

The Gaia Blue-Photometer (BP) and Red-Photometer (RP) spectra are essential for identifying metal-poor stars, which are critical for understanding the chemical evolution of the Galaxy and probing its earliest phases. This study outlines a technique for automatically detecting these stars using the combined data from the blue and red instruments. We define a metal-poor candidate as one that exhibits a metallicity estimate below -0.5 from the red spectra and a signal-to-noise ratio exceeding 20 from the blue spectra. We assess the method's performance by evaluating the purity and completeness of the resulting sample. We also analyze the characteristics of the detected metal-poor stars and compare our findings with recent studies on the spatial and age distribution of the Galaxy's stellar halo.

Global climate change is intensifying wildfire seasons, which now inflict severe economic and ecological damages. To better prepare for the future, it is essential to predict future fire activity and understand the factors driving recent increases in wildfire intensity. This study examines global data on fire intensity, defined as the count of active fires per 100,000 hectares, alongside seasonal indices and environmental variables. We employ a combination of statistical and machine learning models to predict fire intensity, accounting for the non-stationarity of the data. Our findings indicate that the Northern Hemisphere experiences a season extending from May to September, while in the Southern Hemisphere, it runs from October to March. Additionally, we identify a significant link between the strength of the El Niño-Southern Oscillation (ENSO) and fire intensity. To enhance prediction accuracy, we advise incorporating an interaction term between intensity and seasonality alongside ENSO indices. Ultimately, our research underscores the critical role of climate change in predicting fire intensity and offers a robust framework for future modeling.

This study investigates corpus-based morphological complexity metrics, specifically examining their correlations and through a randomized 12-complex corpus. We also perform validation experiments to ensure the reliability of these results.

Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) offers a potential resolution to discrepancies between numerical galaxy simulations and astronomical observations regarding small-scale gravitational potential. This study investigates gravitational lensing by galaxy clusters, specifically examining how SIDM influences the magnification of distant background sources. We utilize the N-body simulation code GADGET-2 to model a standard cosmological scenario, comparing two scenarios: one with cold dark matter (CDM) and another incorporating SIDM via a dark matter halo of $10^{14} M_{\odot}$. Magnification estimates for individual background galaxies are derived using galaxy-light profiles fitted with Sérsien models. Our findings indicate that while the stellar mass of $10^{11} M_{\odot}$ satellite galaxies dominates the lensing effects, SIDM does not significantly alter magnification values at this mass range. However, at lower masses, specifically below $10^{10} M_{\odot}$, we observe that self-interacting dark matter can enhance magnification by a factor of 2 to 3.

Model compression is a critical area of research aimed at reducing the size of models without compromising performance. While existing methods typically assume full state observability, this work investigates model compression under partial state observability. We introduce a technique to identify unobservable states that can be discarded, thereby facilitating model compression. Our approach is validated on two distinct tasks: model compression itself and model merging. In the context of merging, we demonstrate that utilizing our compressed model within the DOVE method yields significant improvements in merging performance.

This article introduces the concept of Absolute-Rotated Kullback-Leibler Divergence (AR-LED). We demonstrate that minimizing the sum of these divergence values across all pairwise combinations of hidden variables yields an optimization approach for Independent Component Analysis (ICA). Consequently, the newly developed algorithm, M-ar-K-Rapid ICA, utilizes iterative updates to compute independent components by addressing this minimization problem. Additionally, the paper includes a numerical simulation demonstrating the method's application in solving ICA.

Social platforms with geo-tags are increasingly utilized to identify incidents like road accidents and natural disasters. While prior research has primarily leveraged user-written descriptions, this paper proposes a novel approach to detect incidents from the location data of user posts. This new method offers a distinct advantage: it does not require annotated statements specifying the nature of an incident. The proposed framework employs deep learning to map the spatio-temporal distribution of locations, automatically isolating clusters that correspond to incidents. By utilizing the Continuous Time Continuous State space (CTCBS) model, we can capture evolving patterns over time. The method's effectiveness is validated through experiments using real-world social media data regarding various incidents, including road accidents, natural disasters, and disease outbreaks.

We establish the existence, uniqueness, and positive bounds for weak solutions to a specific class of elliptic equations involving measure data. This work extends the seminal findings of a prior study by the author.

This study introduces a high-throughput method designed to rapidly identify novel compounds with high abundance of cobalt within the Y-CO-B system. The methodology involves substituting Y and O atoms in known LiCoO2 with varying ratios of Y and Co, followed by a multi-stage process of structure relaxation, phonon dispersion analysis, and DFT calculations. The results reveal that the LaCoO2 structure remains stable across a wide range of Y/Co concentrations. The most favorable configurations feature a Y/Co ratio of 0.75, demonstrating enhanced mechanical properties and a significantly greater density of states near the Fermi level compared to the LiCoO2 reference. The described protocol is versatile and applicable to other material systems for identifying stable binary or multicomponent compounds.

This study addresses risk-conscious bidding in display advertising by developing an adaptive algorithm that adapts to fluctuating market environments. The objective is to maximize advertiser revenue while respecting both a predefined revenue risk threshold and a budget constraint. The core challenge involves simultaneously determining bid prices and selection probabilities for each impression, balancing the desire for high revenue against the need to control risk exposure and adhere to budget limits. To the best of our knowledge, no existing methods fully tackle this specific combination of constraints. We propose an efficient, online, and scalable solution that provides theoretical assurances. The experimental evaluation, conducted on both synthetic data and real-world datasets, demonstrates that our method outperforms current state-of-the-art approaches.

We examine a strategic game where two players, Alice and Bob, receive opposite binary instructions and attempt to coordinate their outputs to both satisfy these opposing goals. Alice aims to match her input with Bob's output, whereas Bob aims to mismatch his input with Alice's. The game's success probability is defined by the average of these conflicting objectives. While classical strategies cannot achieve these goals simultaneously, quantum strategies can, provided the players share a specific type of entangled state. We demonstrate that the minimal negativity of the Wigner quasiprobability distribution required for such quantum strategies is minimized in a single-qubit system. Consequently, we establish a direct link between the efficiency of the guidance problem and the negativity of the Wigner distribution. Additionally, we explore the relationship between quantum nonlocality and this minimal negativity.

This paper introduces a security evaluation method for Quantum Key Distribution (QKD) protocols, the reliability of which hinges on the assumption that random sources are perfectly uniform. We demonstrate that secure key generation remains feasible even when dealing with imperfect, biased sources, provided we apply a specific security evaluation approach. This method involves modeling the biased source as a theoretically perfect uniform random source combined with additive bias noise. By treating the QKD protocol analysis as a function of the derived key generation rate and secret key bit rate—both of which depend on the variance of the bias noise—we establish a security evaluation framework. We validate this method by examining two practical versions of the Decoy State Protocol with Privacy Amplification (DSPPA), specifically analyzing scenarios involving non-uniform random emission sources for the biased device (BSED). Our findings confirm that this evaluation approach is both simple and effective.

This paper investigates the dynamics of timelike Bertrand curves and establishes specific conditions regarding their behavior. We derive the necessary requirements for a curve to possess these properties, providing an alternative proof of the findings presented by B.Y. Chen. The work concludes by presenting concrete examples to illustrate these findings.

This brief article examines combinations of distinct stochastic processes, specifically focusing on diffusion processes and martingale measures. We introduce a class of martingale diffusion processes and subsequently analyze sampling distributions and combinations involving Feller processes. These applications include the Binomial formula and the Poisson formula, as well as the derivation of combinations and sampling configurations involving standard Feller processes and exponential martingales. A particular emphasis is placed on combinations involving the Cram\`eron, Cram\`eron-Feller, and Bellier processes.

This study introduces a diagrammatic framework designed to analyze multi-photon scattering events involving two excited three-level atoms coupled to a one-dimensional lossy transmission line. We demonstrate that the full amplitude for such complex interactions can be constructed by linking smaller amplitudes corresponding to simpler, pairwise scattering events. Furthermore, this approach allows for the derivation of an effective non-Hermitian Hamiltonian that accurately reproduces the results of our theoretical model. This effective Hamiltonian captures the non-Hermitian characteristics inherent in dissipative processes and effectively redefines the concept of probability conservation within this open quantum system context.

We examine the evolution of a universe containing both boosted dark energy and matter, focusing on how spin-dependent transport mechanisms influence the system. Our investigation involves solving the kinetic Boltzmann equation to determine the dynamics of this dark energy scalar field. We find that a significant velocity for the field drives a cosmological evolution resembling a component with equation of state $w = -1/3$. However, when a speed of at least $c$ is required to match observational data, our model falls outside the realm of standard boosted dark energy theories.

This brief article examines the connection between the Faulhaber sum, which covers odd powers of integers up to $n$, and the $n$th Eulerian number. Furthermore, it demonstrates how this sum can be expressed as a polynomial in the sum of the first $n$ integers, $n(n+1)/2$.

Traditional non-coherent differential Continuous Phase Modulation (CPM) detection is constrained by the requirement that it preserve phase continuity across symbol boundaries, which restricts its effective processing delay to the CP M period multiplied by the minimum CPM memory value. This paper introduces a novel non-coherent differential detector that maintains phase continuity while allowing the processing delay to extend up to the sum of the CPM memory value and an additional specified number of symbol durations equal to the CPM period. Leveraging a Markov chain model for CPM, the proposed method generates a maximum likelihood (ML) detector codebook that can be pre-computed and is applicable to any CPM configuration. Simulation results demonstrate that the proposed detector achieves the same bit error probability as the optimal ML differential detector under conditions of higher processing delays.

Reward signals are crucial for guiding agents to achieve their objectives. However, manually crafting rewards is often arduous and labor-intensive, leading many researchers to develop automated, learning-based reward generation methods. A key challenge in automating this process is determining the optimal reward value for each state. A promising strategy involves comparing the current state against a reference state, but this comparison is difficult for humans to execute without a clear visual framework.

To address this, we introduce a cluster-based reward learning framework that is both visually intuitive and effective. In this approach, a batch of reference states is generated and clustered together. For every state, the agent calculates similarity scores with every reference state within the cluster. These scores are then aggregated to produce a final similarity metric between state clusters. This method is particularly advantageous for tasks with complex, high-dimensional state spaces.

We applied this framework to the challenging benchmark of Atari 2D video games. Our evaluation demonstrates that the learned rewards are comparable to handcrafted ones in terms of both quality and the time required to develop them. Furthermore, we observed a marked reduction in user effort when integrating this reward learning system with a visual assistance tool.

The noncommutative framework of space-time is applied to the nucleon's internal structure. The paper derives the noncommutative configuration functions for up and down quarks within the neutron and proton, respectively, utilizing the free propagator as the free system's counterpart. The resulting functions are normalized and compared against their standard commutative equivalents. The analysis concludes that noncommutative space-time alters the internal quark structure of the nucleon, leading to a shift in the configuration functions relative to the commutative case.

This paper investigates the ground state properties and edge behavior of frustrated variants of the Toric code, specifically dimer- and triangler-sublattice-decorated variants. Our findings reveal that the system's bulk remains a four-fold topological spin-liquid, whereas the boundary evolves into a two-fold topological phase. This distinct spin-lattice behavior contrasts with the standard, non-failing code, where both bulk and boundary exhibit four-fold topology. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the system's classification relies on the topology of its underlying substrate, specifically the second homotopy group of its graph structure. This insight allows us to generalize the model to include subjects derived from fullerene-like structures.

This work derives an approximate sigma-model representation for the logarithmic determinant of a simple deformation involving a finite rank perturbation of random band matrices. We establish this sigma-model approximation under specific conditions where the band width scales as $O(N^{-1/2+\delta})$ for $\delta > 0$. Our findings are applicable to the so-called "intricate deformation" framework, which is currently being investigated to analyze the chiral phase transition in Quantum Chromodynamics (QCD).

While pre-trained models have significantly advanced various natural language processing tasks, their effectiveness in handling comprehensive understanding for conversations remains limited. This paper introduces a new approach to fully leverage pre-trained models for complete comprehension of dialogues. We propose a task-specific pre-training strategy that focuses on "meaningful" sentence pairs within dialogues. By utilizing the inherent structure of conversations, our method enhances the contextual capabilities of pre-trained models. Extensive experiments demonstrate that our model, when fine-tuned, achieves state-of-the-art results across multiple dialogue understanding benchmarks.

Although significant strides have been made in developing machine learning models, achieving interpretability remains elusive. While numerous academic studies have attempted to define interpretability, the field lacks a unified, standard framework. Consequently, this paper introduces a new framework that evaluates algorithmic interpretability through the lens of human learning processes. By doing so, we provide a new way to measure and understand interpretability that is grounded in how humans acquire knowledge. This new method was used to measure the interpretability of 110 algorithms from 14 different families. Our results show that traditional measures struggle to capture nuances, particularly within algorithm families where performance varies. To address this, we propose the Intricacy Score for Algorithms (ICA), which quantifies the complexity of an algorithm based on human learning theory. Our findings reveal that an algorithm's ICA score strongly predicts its performance, and that this score offers a more precise assessment of interpretability than previous methods.

In response to the growing demand for compact and efficient machine learning models, this paper introduces TiWS-iForest, an optimized version of the Isolation Forest algorithm. Designed for constrained environments, TiWS-iForest addresses two critical challenges: the need for a highly space-efficient implementation and the requirement for a weak guidance function to maintain effective anomaly detection. The proposed approach is validated across three distinct use cases: (1) a TinyML deployment on a microcontroller, (2) a distributed simulation under resource-limited conditions, and (3) a centralized simulation. Experimental results demonstrate that TiWS-iForest achieves an anomaly detection performance comparable to the original Isolation Forest, while significantly reducing memory consumption by 90% and lowering computational overhead by 50%.

This study proposes reprioritizing the commonly used inhomogeneous Poisson process under the framework of transformed time, specifically via the power transformation method introduced by Kijima (2000). Adopting a Bayesian perspective, we derive the corresponding posterior distributions for both the inhomogeneous Poisson process intensity function and the transformation's power parameter. Our objective is to evaluate this new approach against standard methods through a comparison of numerical results from two distinct real-world datasets.

The concept of average flux cross-section, denoted as $\bar{\sigma}_f(E) = \frac{\int_V \sigma_f(\vec{r}, E) \phi(\vec{r}, E) dV}{\int_V \phi(\vec{r}, E) dV}$, is introduced to quantify reaction rates within an irradiated material. This work demonstrates that functions of average flux cross-section exhibit local extrema in specific regions. We establish that in areas where neutron flux is spatially uniform, these average cross-section functions exhibit stationary behavior. Additionally, under conditions of reflection symmetry, the functions display stationary points at the axis of symmetry. We also identify that in regionally averaged contexts, these functions reach their maximum values. These findings offer valuable insights regarding the reliability and precision inherent in average flux cross-section measurements.

This article introduces the COMET-ATOMIC 2020 challenge, the inaugural competition dedicated to evaluating models for online common sense reasoning. Participants were assessed on their ability to extend the existing ATOMIC knowledge graph by establishing new relations among entities. To achieve this, models had to integrate a symbolic reasoning approach with knowledge distillation from a large-scale neural architecture trained on common sense data. We also detail the evaluation of a proposed hybrid model that merges these symbolic and neural strategies, demonstrating that our system attained state-of-the-art results on the benchmark.

The Hi-GAL survey, conducted using the JCMT's SCUBA-2 instrument, targets cold molecular gas and dust within the Galactic Plane. It captures data across three wavelengths—450, 850, and 450 microns—utilizing filter sets that offer both high spectral resolution and sensitivity. This paper details the information reduction pipeline employed to generate the survey's data products. These outputs encompass calibrated images, maps of spectral energy distributions (SEDs), and catalogue entries for point sources. Additionally, this document outlines the survey's current status and outlines future initiatives, specifically addressing the creation of a comprehensive catalogue for extended sources.

We present new high-resolution spectroscopy of NGC 2808, a massive globular cluster, focusing on Fe, Mg, Al, Si, Ca, Na, and Ti abundances. Our study targets 15 stars with effective temperatures between 4,000 K and 9,000 K to ensure a comprehensive coverage of the main sequence. By analyzing these data, we confirm a significant metallicity spread within the cluster's main sequence. Our findings indicate that metal-rich stars are more abundant than metal-poor ones, with the most significant differences observed in the range of 4,500 K < T_eff < 7,500 K. This trend is consistent with earlier investigations of the cluster. Additionally, we found that metal-rich stars outnumber their metal-poor counterparts across the entire main sequence, a result that aligns with previous studies.

Single file movement is characterized by the inability of particles to pass one another, with its dynamics heavily dependent on the boundary setup. This study examines a system of non-interacting Brownian particles confined to one dimension under an entropic barrier at the exit, where the system's entropy decreases as particles attempt to leave. We analyze the statistics regarding particles' initial exit times and their subsequent residence durations. Results indicate that the probability density for the initial exit time follows a $t^{-3/2}$ scaling, matching that of a system with free boundaries. However, the system's exit duration statistics are significantly altered by the entropic barrier; specifically, the probability density for the duration scales as $t^{-1+\alpha}$, where $\alpha$ is a parameter between 0 and 1. This exponent is determined by the entropic barrier's slope and the position of the exiting particle relative to the system's center. We further explore the correlations between exit times for different particles and explore how these correlations are influenced by the entropic barrier. Finally, we discuss the broader implications of these findings for other systems exhibiting single file movement.

Quantum probability theory, which is built on Hilbert space, is the foundation of the current mathematical framework for describing physical phenomena in the quantum realm. Measurement within this system is inherently probabilistic, meaning that the probability of a specific outcome is determined by the state of the system prior to the act of measurement. We have developed a generalized form of Quantum Bayes' Theorem designed to demonstrate the internal consistency of inferences regarding measurements across successive steps. This theorem serves as the direct quantum counterpart to Bayesian probability theory, functioning as the basis for updating the state of a quantum system following a measurement. Additionally, we have established a generalized form of the "trace rule" within this context. This rule ensures that the probability of a specific outcome remains constant regardless of whether it is calculated using the pre-measurement or post-measurement state, thereby confirming the consistency of measurement inferences.

The equation of state for a finite system is expressed as a series expansion in terms of cumulative cumulants, where each term represents a specific combination of pressure variations within the system. For a given volume, the $n$-th order term in this series is directly linked to pressure fluctuations occurring at that specific level. Applying this theoretical framework to the hadron resonance gas (HGR) model, we find that the leading-order term effectively reproduces the HGR's equation of state down to a particle count of $N \approx 100$. Beyond this threshold, higher-order contributions become significant, necessitating their inclusion for accuracy. Furthermore, the study examines how the HGR equation of state deviates from the ideal gas approximation as system size increases.

The primary goal of this memo is the explicit computation of a specific category within the cohomology rings of an algebra governing Steenrod operations. While foundational work by various authors has established that these objects are non-trivial, here we provide concrete formulas for the corresponding cycles and a set of representative chains. These results are derived as a direct application of the Kudo transgression theorem, which connects the cohomology of maximal ideal fiber spaces to that of the algebra's odd-dimensional exterior algebra.

This work introduces the ideal distributed control framework for general- symmetric time-varying multi-agent systems. By leveraging the graph symmetry, the proposed approach utilizes a single sensor per agent to design a filter-based distributed controller that ensures the entire network achieves consensus. Specifically, the control input for each agent is determined by the output of a graph filter applied to the local measurements of the agents holding the initial values. This method offers two primary benefits: (1) the resulting distributed filter is significantly simpler to design than traditional protocols, as the protocol coefficients for standard consensus protocols are directly derived from the filter's parameters; and (2) the approach for generating distributed controllers is more flexible and readily adaptable to practical scenarios. Furthermore, the presented protocol is highly efficient for standard network topologies, as it only requires the local neighborhood information of the agents. This study also examines the scalability of the proposed protocol in terms of communication and computational complexity. Finally, the effectiveness of this strategy is demonstrated through a simulation example.

The widespread adoption of video sharing platforms has created a pressing need for efficient video retrieval systems. Although current search engines primarily rely on textual queries, there is a growing demand for dynamic picture-based search, enabling users to find videos by dragging and dropping images. This study introduces a new dynamic picture indexing approach that leverages interest point descriptors and a query image normalization technique. These methods enhance the robustness of dynamic scene indexing against variations in scale, rotation, and lighting. The system's effectiveness was validated through comprehensive testing on the widely used UCSD Datasets, demonstrating that the proposed method outperforms existing state-of-the-art techniques.

This study examines how the transport uniformity of particles in a driven sawtooth-like potential depends on their driving speed and the strength of the ripples within that potential. The research reveals that the nature of transport shifts based on the ratio of the particles' energy to the energy of the sawtooth potential. Specifically, when a particle's energy is lower than the potential's, the transport remains highly consistent; however, as the particle's energy exceeds the potential's, the transport uniformity decreases significantly.

This study proposes a novel method for estimating impulse response functions following shocks in a multivariate time series. The approach utilizes local projections to isolate the immediate impact of a surprise innovation from its lingering effects. The author establishes asymptotic properties and finite-sample performance metrics, demonstrating that the technique outperforms conventional methods in simulations. The paper concludes by applying the method to a dataset comprising 200 years of US macroeconomic data to examine how various shocks influence key economic variables.

This work examines the angular momentum of the quantum vacuum, or quantum Casimir momentum, generated by a magnetic field in the presence of an electric charge subject to Landau quantization. The analysis covers both the scenario of an isolated charge and one embedded in a spherical shell of radius $R$. It is demonstrated that the angular momentum of the quantum void in the first excited state of the Landau level exceeds that of the semi-classical limit by a term proportional to $\hbar$. Furthermore, the study explores the implications of these findings for the angular momentum composition of an electron.

Named entity recognition (NER) is a crucial natural language processing (NLP) task that involves identifying pre-defined entities within text. Although hyperbolic spaces have proven effective for representing hierarchical structures, current methods are limited to learning embeddings for well-known entities, leaving unknown entities unrepresented. To address this limitation, we introduce FGNET-RH, a novel fine-grained NER framework that operates within a hyperbolic space. This approach leverages a unified, refined hyperbolic space to model both known and unknown fine-grained classes by learning mappings from coarse-to-fine hierarchical taxonomies. FGNET-RH employs a multi-collinear tensor network to model sequential text patterns and integrates a multi-collinear tensor-based entity classifier to handle multi-level classification. Comprehensive experiments on five fine-grained NER benchmarks demonstrate that FGNET-RH outperforms state-of-the-art methods, achieving gains of +0.20 F1-score on the FGNET-RH dataset and +0.20 on the FB15I-8R dataset.

This paper focuses on the subclass $\mathcal{U}\subset\mathcal{S}$, which encompasses univalent functions $f(z)=z+\sum_{n=2}^{\infty}a_nz^n$ on the unit disk $\mathbb{D}$ that satisfy the condition $|a_2a_n-a_n| \leq 2$ for all $n\geq 3$. The study derives the sharp upper bounds for the second Hankel determinant, $H_2(2,n)$, when restricted to this class. The findings are then broadened to a broader class of functions, denoted as $\mathcal{G}$, which includes the subclass $\mathcal{U}$. Additionally, sharp bounds for $H_2(2,n)$ are established for the general class $\mathcal{G}$. The obtained results are novel and improve upon several existing findings in the literature.

In contemporary cloud data centers, the surge in users and requests necessitates a robust demand for Virtual Machines (VMs). To accommodate this, data centers increasingly rely on VM reservation strategies to guarantee specific resource availability for clients. However, these guaranteed allocations can restrict the cloud provider's ability to accept additional workloads, potentially reducing overall revenue. This paper introduces a new approach called "PrePartition," designed to optimize the distribution of reserved VMs. By leveraging this method, providers can maintain better load distribution while ensuring that reservations are fulfilled. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm ensures an optimal outcome for every reservation request. Experimental results indicate that Prepartition outperforms existing methods in terms of both load balancing and the success rate of fulfilling reservation requests.

We introduce a novel deep learning framework designed to forecast Nash equilibria in dynamic games of incomplete information. By leveraging the Kuhn algorithm, we first derive Bayes-Nash equilibria for specific instances to train a specialized classifier. This component identifies the determining features of game parameters that yield equilibrium, even when those parameters themselves remain hidden. Subsequently, a fixed-point network is employed to verify the classified solution, ensuring the final prediction satisfies equilibrium conditions. We demonstrate that this approach delivers highly accurate equilibrium forecasts across diverse and complex game structures.

This work investigates the asymptotic behavior of estimated causal effects within a framework where the propensity score and outcome regression functions are nonparametrically estimated. We establish that the causal effect estimator exhibits the same convergence rate as the smoother of the relevant outcome regression and the log-estimator of the propensity score. To achieve this, we adopt a high-dimensional setup that imposes no constraints on the dimensions of the covariate spaces for either the treatment or control groups, nor on the number of basis functions utilized for outcome modeling. Although the treatment and control processes are assumed to be independent conditional on the covariates, the analysis remains valid even when these conditions are not strictly met. These theoretical findings are demonstrated through simulations and an empirical analysis of data from a randomized clinical trial concerning the association between treatment dosage and survival duration.

This study addresses the challenge of anticipating cyber-physical assaults within stealthy constraints using only historical data. We propose a method that integrates two components: a traditional predictive approach and a novel system-specific approach. The traditional method relies on historical inputs and state estimates to generate forecasts, but it is susceptible to initial state estimation errors. In contrast, the novel approach leverages the system's mathematical model to predict future states based on prior data, thereby mitigating errors stemming from uncertain initial conditions. We demonstrate that incorporating this system-specific method significantly enhances the accuracy of predictive surveillance. Furthermore, we show its practical application in detecting and identifying attacks within cyber-physical systems.

This study presents GAE-ISumm, an unmonitored zero-shot summarization model for Indian languages. We introduce a novel dataset, ISUMM, which contains English summaries for selected Indian languages. By integrating this data with a cross-lingual pre-trained model, we train GAE-ISumm. This architecture utilizes a multilingual encoder trained on a large corpus covering 14 language pairs, alongside a language-independent attention mechanism. Our experiments demonstrate that GAE-ISumm achieves state-of-the-art performance on the newly introduced summ dataset, while our analysis of the model's internal representations offers valuable insights for future multilingual pre-trained encoders.

This work examines the analog of a thick, spherical design of dimension 2 and dimension 3 that adheres to the Noether constraints in rank 2 and rank 3, respectively, within the framework of Noetherian S-rings. The findings demonstrate that the intersection numbers $a_2$ in a Noetherian S-ring $S$ of rank 2 and positive integer $m$ must satisfy $a_2 = m-1$ or $a_2 = m-2$, provided the characteristic of the underlying abelian group is not 2. Furthermore, every such pair $(m, a_2)$ is shown to be realizable. For Noetherian S-rings $S$ with rank 3 and positive integer $m$, the third eigenvalue of the adjacency matrix $A_3$ must be either $m-1$ or $A_3 = m-2$, with the exception of the case where $A_3 = m-2$ and the subgroup $H$ is elementary abelian of order 4. In this scenario, we demonstrate that the pair $(m, A_3)$ is always realizable.

Recent studies have demonstrated that Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) can be reformulated as Bayesian linear regression problems, a perspective that has enabled researchers to derive closed-form closed-form solutions for VAEs employing Gaussian priors and likelihoods. Building upon this foundation, our work extends these analytical, closed-form solutions to cases where both priors and likelihoods follow uniform distributions within a specified radius, resulting in a model we term the "square VAE." Our investigation reveals that this square VAE exhibits regularization properties that constrain the encoder's representation space, thereby reducing the model's susceptibility to overfitting. Consequently, we propose integrating a regularization term into the square VAE's objective function to further mitigate these overfitting risks. Empirical evaluations across various datasets confirm that this enhanced model consistently outperforms standard VAEs.

The rapid proliferation of Internet of Things (IoT) devices has significantly increased security risks, particularly within the home environment. This study introduces a novel private blockchain framework designed to bolster IoT security by integrating intelligent monitoring and location tracking. The proposed system utilizes a consensus mechanism that merges Proof of Work (PoW) with Proof of Authority (PoA) to ensure data integrity. The framework was evaluated using nodes on Amazon Web Services (AWS) cloud infrastructure, with comparative analysis conducted against systems built on public blockchains and systems lacking blockchain technology entirely. Results indicate that the suggested private blockchain solution offers superior performance and enhanced security compared to these alternative approaches.

This paper introduces a deep learning-based approach to quantize L-values in soft-decoding, utilizing a single feed-forward neural network to map real values to the required 2^N - 1 discrete levels of Gray coding. The method is demonstrated on a (15, 7) Hamming code with N=4 and achieves a performance gain of approximately 0.2 dB compared to conventional binary magnitude quantization, alongside significant reductions in computational complexity.

A directed planar graph is classified as upward if its edges can be mapped to curves rising monotonically without crossing, where this monotonicity applies specifically to the upward direction. This study introduces and analyzes the parameterized complexity landscape for determining upward planarity, focusing on constraints related to vertex degree and the count of edges requiring specific orientations. Our findings demonstrate that these parameterized problems are fixed-parameter tractable, provided we also account for constraints on the count of edges requiring specific orientations. Our approach involves refining the existing linear-time algorithm for upward planarity testing with a parameterized component that leverages graph minors. This method yields a problem that is fixed-parameter tractable with respect to a combination of parameters representing vertex degree and required edge orientations. Furthermore, we establish that the problem remains W[1]-hard when parameterized solely by vertex degree, indicating inherent computational difficulty under this specific constraint.

Crowdsourced data is increasingly common, yet it often suffers from inconsistencies, contradictions, and inaccuracies. This paper introduces an unsupervised approach to identify and eliminate erroneous entries in such datasets without relying on external validation. By constructing "human softmax" distributions for each item based on varied crowd annotations, we calculate specific entropy measures to quantify customer uncertainty. These metrics serve as predictors for labeling error. We then utilize a sampling strategy to determine the likelihood that any given label is incorrect and conditionally remove it. The proposed method was tested on two distinct datasets: one containing label error predictions and another consisting of musical genre classifications. Results demonstrate that the algorithm effectively identifies and rectifies labeling mistakes across both cases.

We demonstrate that $C^r$ ($r\ge2$) Anosov flows on closed 3-manifolds exhibit a diminishing normal range for their Dataov-Sullivan and Dolgopyat-Danforth transfer operators when acting on spaces of $C^{r}$ functions. This finding enables an extension of the $r=1$ result provided in [10] (specifically, the work of the same authors), establishing norm decay for their specific family of transfer operators associated with $C^{r}$ ($r\ge2$) time-1 maps. As a direct implication, we obtain enhanced spectral gap estimates for the one-step transfer operators of all previously studied $C^{r}$ ($r\ge2$) Anhosv flows. Furthermore, we generalize the original proof from [10] to cover a broader category of transfer operators linked to both periodic and non-periodic semi-flows.

This paper investigates $n$-player games characterized by two key features: the payoffs for each player depend on the actions of all participants, and the strategy profile of every player is perfectly correlated with the strategies chosen by the others. While the first condition defines a nonlocal game, the second implies that the players' moves share a common randomness source, effectively turning the nonlocal contest into a single-player decision problem. We demonstrate that within the subclass of these games where players act to maximize their expected utility, the scenario involving "tight" or maximally correlated states is fully integrable with respect to the players' choices. Our proof relies on a specific duality between the games played under correlated maximum randomness and the nonlocal contests defined by Bellking testings. This result confirms that, in such games, the Nash equilibrium can be effectively computed.

In high-temperature cuprate superconductors, the vortex lattice undergoes a melting transition into a vortex fluid as the applied magnetic field ($B$) increases. We present evidence that an intermediate grid state exists between this lattice and fluid, characterized by both a higher vortex density and distinct disorder compared to the lattice. Our findings indicate that this vortex grid is stable over a substantial range of fields, commencing at relatively low fields where vortex interactions are weak.

The flow of thermal photons emitted during heavy-ion collisions serves as a precise probe of the QGP's evolution and transport properties. We have calculated the flow velocity of thermal photons by utilizing a thermal and flow separation framework within the QCD effective kinetic theory. Our findings indicate that the flow velocity peaks at an intermediate specific shear viscosity ($\eta/s$) value, a result that stems from the distinct temperature dependencies of thermal photon sources. Consequently, measuring the flow velocity across different centrality levels could enable the determination of the QCD specific viscosity. Furthermore, this $\eta/s$ value provides valuable insights into the QCD phase diagram, potentially aiding in the discovery of a critical point.

This study employs a mean-field model to investigate the magnetic ordering of systems based on triangular and kagome lattices, where interactions are limited to nearest neighbors. The analysis reveals that the model supports both collinear and non-collinear ground states, contingent upon the ratio of antiferromagnetic to ferromagnetic coupling strengths. Specifically, when antiferromagnetic interactions dominate, the system adopts a 120-degree ordered configuration; conversely, a precessional state emerges when ferromagnetic effects are more significant. Furthermore, we demonstrate that by adjusting the relative interaction strengths, the order of magnetic alignment can be switched between these two distinct ground states.

This study addresses intervention effect identification in large-scale experiments, specifically focusing on scenarios with extensive sets of interventions and dependent outcomes. We introduce a novel, data-driven false discovery rate (FDR) control method applicable to general large-scale inference problems involving intervention effects. This approach accommodations outcome dependence, heterogeneous variances, and non-normal distributions, while ensuring statistical power remains high. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework through simulations and a real-world application.

We present a new expansion law applicable to all celestial bodies within the solar system, solar system, and universe. We demonstrate that gravitational attraction is not exclusively inversely proportional to the square of the distance; a additional repulsive force emerges when a specific threshold distance is exceeded. This added force drives the accelerated cosmic expansion, resolves the horizon problem, and accounts for the varying expansion rates of the universe, large-scale voids, and galaxies.

We investigate the type-X two-Higgs-doublet model (2HDM) in the context of the recently observed tension between experimental measurements of the $W$ boson mass and Standard Model predictions. We demonstrate that the observed deviation can be accommodated by the 2HDM, which also provides an explanation for the persistent divergence in the muon $g-2$ measurement. Specifically, the required tension is resolved by a combination of a lower bound on the top quark Yukawa coupling and an enhancement of the bottom quark Yukawa coupling. The resulting parameter space is examined with respect to LHC Run 2 constraints, the latest LHCb results on $W$ mass, and the most recent data from Fermilab's Muon $g-2$ experiment. We find that the compatibility of these constraints is highly sensitive to the top quark Yukawa coupling, which is strictly bounded from below. The most permissive upper limit on the magnitude of the top Yukawa coupling is approximately $0.5$.

Query rephrasing is a well-established technique for enhancing the retrieval of related concepts, yet it typically relies on expert knowledge, which is expensive and difficult to obtain. This study introduces a cost-effective, automated method for generating queries by drawing on crowd wisdom. We hypothesize that a broad, non-expert audience can provide valuable, actionable insights that enhance query rephrasing. To test this, we developed a framework that allows crowd-derived perspectives to inform an automatic query rewriting process. Our findings demonstrate that utilizing these crowd insights significantly improves the accuracy of retrieved concepts.

This paper introduces a novel, unsupervised deep neural network method for measuring speech-to-speech and speech-to-text synchronization distances in conversational contexts. Our proposed framework consists of two distinct stages: first, we align consecutive speech turns using a sequence-to-sequence deep neural network; second, we compute the synchronization distance by comparing a reference transcription against the aligned actual utterances. To ensure robustness, we evaluate our model using both simulated delays and real-world conversational data. The results demonstrate that our approach successfully recovers the relative timing of real conversations and accurately estimates the time-delay effect. Furthermore, our method significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art techniques.

We introduce the release version of resourceful color scale error depiction v2 (RCSEDv2), an open-source suite designed to visualize both spectral and imaging data. This version features an expanded library of over 100 color scales, including newly added categories for perceptual uniformity. To facilitate the validation and comparison of these diverse color scales, we have developed a suite of online utilities that are part of the RCSEDv2 framework. These tools enable users to view preprocessed image data, input custom images, and select from a vast repository of available color scales. All functionalities are accessible via https://astro-ubc.github.io/RCSEDv2/.

Recent deep learning approaches have demonstrated significant potential in temporal action segmentation (TAS), yet they are heavily reliant on extensive labeled data, rendering them impractical for scenarios where annotation is unavailable. Addressing this limitation, we introduce Self-supervised Supervised Caption Action Parsing (SSCAP), a method designed to execute TAS effectively without requiring any labeled information. SSCAP operates by first generating dense action caption predictions for every frame across an action set, followed by a pooling mechanism that aggregates these captions to construct a self-supervised learning objective. Experimental evaluations across three action segmentation benchmarks confirm that our framework eliminates the need for labeled data while substantially outperforming both prior self-supervised techniques and standard supervised baselines. Furthermore, the source code can be accessed at \url{https://github.com/zhenguo99/sscap}.
